questions.prompt: An npn BJT consists of which sequence of regions?
options: p emitter, n base, p collector
n emitter, n base, p collector
n emitter, p base, n collector
p emitter, p base, n collector
questions.explanation: npn names the three regions in order: an n-type emitter, a thin p-type base, and an n-type collector (reader Sec. 11.2.1).

questions.prompt: In the npn symbol, what does the arrow on the emitter show?
options: The direction electrons flow in the emitter
Which terminal is the base
The direction of the base current
The direction of conventional emitter current in forward-active operation (out of the device)
questions.explanation: The arrow points out of the emitter for an npn (conventional current leaves there); for a pnp it points in.

questions.prompt: Why is the emitter doped much more heavily than the base?
options: So that almost all of the emitter-base current is carried by electrons injected into the base, not holes injected back into the emitter
To reduce the collector capacitance
So the base is easy to contact
To make the base-collector junction break down at low voltage
questions.explanation: The injected hole current into the emitter scales as \(1/N_E\), while the useful electron current scales as \(1/N_B\). \(N_E \gg N_B\) makes the base current small and the gain large (reader Sec. 11.5).

questions.prompt: Why must the base be thin compared with the minority-carrier diffusion length?
options: So the base resistance is low
So electrons injected from the emitter cross it before they recombine
To make the base-emitter junction a good capacitor
So holes can tunnel from the collector
questions.explanation: If \(W_B \ll L_n\), almost every injected electron diffuses across and is swept into the collector; few recombine, so the base current stays small.

questions.prompt: In forward-active operation, \(I_C \approx -I_E\). A BJT has \(I_E = -2.004\ \mathrm{mA}\) (flowing out of the emitter) and \(I_C = 2.000\ \mathrm{mA}\). What is the base current in µA?
questions.explanation: KCL: \(I_B = -I_E - I_C = 2.004 - 2.000\ \mathrm{mA} = 4\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) (reader Eq. 11.8). The base current is a tiny difference of two nearly equal currents.

questions.prompt: In the actual (vertical) BJT cross-section, where is the emitter?
options: A buried layer at the bottom of the wafer
Beside the collector, at the same depth
A small n+ region at the surface, inside the p base, which itself sits inside the n collector
Underneath the collector
questions.explanation: Fabrication builds the device from the top: the collector is the n region, the base is diffused into it, and the emitter is diffused into the base (reader Sec. 11.2.2).

questions.prompt: Swapping the collector and emitter connections of a real BJT gives a much lower current gain. Why?
options: The base contact only touches the emitter side
Holes cannot flow toward the collector
The arrow in the symbol defines the physics
The device is not symmetric: the emitter is heavily doped and small, the collector lightly doped and large
questions.explanation: The physical structure is optimized for one direction. Used in reverse, the lightly doped 'emitter' injects many holes back and the gain collapses (reverse-active \(\alpha_R\) is small).

questions.prompt: For a pnp BJT in forward-active operation, which carriers cross the base?
options: Holes injected from the p emitter
Electrons injected from the emitter
Holes injected from the collector
Electrons from the base contact
questions.explanation: Everything mirrors: a p emitter injects holes into the n base, and they diffuse to the p collector.

questions.prompt: An npn has \(I_C = 0.75\ \mathrm{mA}\) and \(I_B = 5\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). What is the magnitude of the emitter current in mA?
questions.explanation: KCL around the device: \(|I_E| = I_C + I_B = 0.75 + 0.005 = 0.755\ \mathrm{mA}\). The emitter carries both the collector and the base current.

questions.prompt: Preview of BJT I-V: which voltage mainly controls the collector current of an npn in forward-active?
options: \(V_{CE}\), linearly
\(V_{BE}\), exponentially
\(V_{CB}\), exponentially
\(V_{BE}\), linearly
questions.explanation: \(I_C \approx I_S e^{V_{BE}/V_{th}}\) (reader Eq. 11.3). \(V_{CE}\) has only a weak effect once the device is in forward-active.
questions.figure_alt: Collector current versus base-emitter voltage: an exponential that is negligible below about 0.6 V and then rises steeply.

questions.prompt: Preview of BJT I-V: with \(I_S = 2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{A}\) and \(V_{th} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), what is \(I_C\) at \(V_{BE} = 0.70\ \mathrm{V}\) (in mA)?
Preview of transistor action: in an npn, why do electrons injected into the base end up in the collector rather than leaving through the base contact?
options: The base contact is insulated
The collector is at a lower potential than the base
They diffuse across the thin base, and the reverse-biased base-collector junction's field sweeps them into the collector
They recombine and are re-emitted
questions.explanation: Diffusion carries them across the base; at the collector junction the field pulls minority electrons through, as in reverse-bias leakage but with a huge supply of carriers.
